category_title: Elementary students with pragmatic language impairments who struggle with turn-taking and engagement
minimal_context: James is sitting on the carpet playing a matching card game with word cards.
dialogue:
TUTOR: Let's play our matching card game on the carpet. We will take turns finding word cards that go together, like 'side' and 'walk'.

STUDENT: (Jumps onto his knees and grabs two cards that go together) I found a match!

TUTOR: Yes, they go together, but it is not your turn. You have to return the cards to the floor.

STUDENT: (Returns the cards to the floor and crosses his arms)

TUTOR: We need to keep playing. Please sit up and look at the cards.

STUDENT: (Rolls onto his back, keeping his arms crossed, and completely ignores the other students and the game)

options.A: Provide written feedback using a 3-point Likert-type scale ranging from 1 (needs improvement) to 3 (great job) at the end of each card game session.
options.B: Modify the card game to fit a direct instruction format with specific components: learning objective, starter activity, modeled instruction, guided practice, independent practice, assessment, and closing activity.
options.C: Tell the student that in group games, we take turns: when someone is taking a turn, it is his turn to watch; when they stop, it is his turn to play.
options.D: Have the student complete reflective journal entries in which he is encouraged to write or draw freely about his experience during the card game.
